newsitem.title: GERMANY: European telecoms rules said to favour monopolies.
newsitem.headline: European telecoms rules said to favour monopolies.

text.p: European telecommunications industry officials on Tuesday complained that with just half a year to go before the sector is opened to full competition, former state phone monopolies still have an unfair advantage.

Newcomers are investing heavily in order to break into a sector that has been dominated for a century by a few largely state-owned bureaucracies, but many warn that regulators are still protecting the monopolies.
"The incumbent operators have a very large natural advantage," said David Ball, European chief executive for Northern Telecom, the Canadian telecoms operator.
"Germany, France and a number of other countries are not demonstrating seriousness about liberalisation," Ball told Reuters on the sidelines of a telecoms conference in Bonn.
There are two main issues that industry executives said were hindering liberalisation.
First, few countries are taking an active regulatory role.

Instead of using the law to force open markets and set the terms of competition, countries like Germany require newcomers to hold negotiations with incumbent monopolies and then to file a complaint if dissatisfied before the regulator gets involved.
The process is time-consuming and plays into the hands of the dominant carrier who can use such negotiations to delay the introduction of competition.

Secondly, the main obstacle to competition remains the issue of interconnection or how and at what cost competitors can use the telephone lines of dominant carriers in order to gain access to businesses and homes in local networks.
"Interconnection negotiations are dragging on," said Hermann Kraemer, board member of German energy group Veba AG, which operates the O.Tel.O joint venture with utility RWE AG.
Interconnection charges are the costs that can make or break a newcomer's business plan. Internationally the average charge is around two pfennigs per minute.
"The regulatory agency in France has already set interconnection charges and they are at this level," Kraemer said. "But the latest offer of Deutsche Telekom AG is more than six pfennig per minute."
O.Tel.O and Arcor Telecommunications, the joint venture led by Mannesmann and the German railway, have filed regulatory complaints against Deutsche Telekom.
